title: Every wrong statement names its error
statement: In a select-all item, every wrong statement must contain an error that can be named, because a statement that is merely less good is not false.
detail: One generator's failure analysis quotes the judge failing a select-all option that was not clearly false, only a mischaracterization. Its fix tells the writer that wrong answers in a select-all item must be false statements, not misleading but plausible ones: for each, the writer completes a sentence naming the specific error, and one it can't complete is too ambiguous. Select-all items passed 40% in that benchmark, their key issue being that they had been written as single-answer items.
against: in an earlier batch, a model's review of 8 such items passed all 8 where the writer's own model, judging, passed 5, and called that judge too strict.

evidence.quote: MSQ | 40% | CRITICAL: Wrong format (4 options, 1 answer instead of 5/2-3)
Option B is NOT clearly factually incorrect - it's more of a mischaracterization/distractor
In MSQ, wrong answers must be STATEMENTS THAT ARE FALSE, not "misleading but plausible."
If you cannot complete that sentence, the statement is too ambiguous.
The two untrue statements are FALSIFIABLE directly from the text — a child can point at the sentence that proves them wrong. Never merely unlikely, never outside the passage.
Refine sets are 6 statements each, 4 true + 2 incorrect, all falsifiable from the text.
